steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write a short introduction for our paper on a self-consistency-style decoding method that makes open-ended LLM responses more factual. Briefly explain decoding and hallucination, the idea behind sampling-based consistency, why existing self consistency doesn't cover full responses, and what we contribute.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. How LLMs decode, and hallucination
2. Sampled responses disagree on hallucinated details
3. Self consistency and its limitation
4. Our contribution

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Decoding and hallucination
- LLM predicts token probabilities, conditioned on prompt + previous output tokens
- decoding strategy (greedy, beam search, nucleus sampling) selects tokens, assembles output string
- like any abstractive generative model: risk of false/unsupported info w.r.t. context or closed book knowledge = hallucination

2. Sampling observation (recent work)
- multiple sampled responses tend to hallucinate different values for each detail
- details shared across samples likely true

3. Self consistency
- when short answer easily parsed from response: vote with exact matches of parsed answer
- more reliable than an individual sample
- does not apply when the full response is needed

4. Contribution
- novel decoding mechanism for any LLM task: sample multiple outputs, pick most consistent choice per sentence
- compare with baselines on automatic factuality metrics; Llama 2 (chat), Mistral
- human evaluations, coarse classification of errors
- code: implementation of method + baselines, human evaluation dataset

A large language model (LLM) generates output text by predicting probabilities for each token, conditioned on a prompt and on the previous tokens in the output. It then uses a decoding strategy like greedy decoding, beam search, or nucleus sampling to select tokens at each position and assemble an output string. LLMs, like any abstractive generative model, risk outputting information that is false or unsupported with respect to a context or closed book knowledge, which is commonly called hallucination.

Recent work has observed that when multiple responses are sampled from a large language model, they are likely to hallucinate different values for each detail. On the other hand, the details that multiple sampled responses have in common are likely to be true.

- when short answer easily parsed from response: vote with exact matches of parsed answer
- more reliable than an individual sample
- does not apply when the full response is needed

- novel decoding mechanism for any LLM task: sample multiple outputs, pick most consistent choice per sentence
- compare with baselines on automatic factuality metrics; Llama 2 (chat), Mistral
- human evaluations, coarse classification of errors
- code: implementation of method + baselines, human evaluation dataset

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
A large language model (LLM) generates output text by predicting probabilities for each token, conditioned on a prompt and on the previous tokens in the output. It then uses a decoding strategy like greedy decoding, beam search, or nucleus sampling to select tokens at each position and assemble an output string. LLMs, like any abstractive generative model, risk outputting information that is false or unsupported with respect to a context or closed book knowledge, which is commonly called hallucination.

Recent work has observed that when multiple responses are sampled from a large language model, they are likely to hallucinate different values for each detail. On the other hand, the details that multiple sampled responses have in common are likely to be true.

When a short answer can easily be parsed from a generated response, a method called self consistency uses voting (with exact matches of the parsed short answer) to pick a better answer, more reliably than using an individual sample. But this procedure does not work for tasks where the full response is needed, and not just an extracted short answer.

Our main contribution is a new decoding mechanism that can be applied to any LLM task. It samples multiple text outputs from the LLM and selects the most consistent choice for each sentence, which reflects what the responses have in common. We compare our decoding technique to several baselines using automatic factuality metrics, applied to Llama 2 (chat) and Mistral. We also contribute human evaluations, including a coarse classification of errors. The accompanying code has an implementation of our method and of the baselines, along with the human evaluation dataset.

It then uses a decoding strategy like greedy decoding, beam search, or nucleus sampling to select tokens at each position and assemble an output string. LLMs, like any abstractive generative model, risk outputting information that is false or unsupported with respect to a context or closed book knowledge, which is commonly called hallucination [1,2,3].

Recent work has observed that when multiple responses are sampled from a large language model, they are likely to hallucinate different values for each detail [3,4]. On the other hand, the details that multiple sampled responses have in common are likely to be true.

When a short answer can easily be parsed from a generated response, self consistency [4] uses voting (with exact matches of the parsed short answer) to pick a better answer, more reliably than using an individual sample. But this procedure does not work for tasks where the full response is needed, and not just an extracted short answer.

Our main contribution is a new decoding mechanism that can be applied to any LLM task. It samples multiple text outputs from the LLM and selects the most consistent choice for each sentence, which reflects what the responses have in common. We compare our decoding technique to several baselines using automatic factuality metrics, applied to Llama 2 (chat) and Mistral. We also contribute human evaluations, including a coarse classification of errors. The accompanying code has an implementation of our method and of the baselines, along with the human evaluation dataset.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
A large language model (LLM) generates output text by predicting probabilities for each token, conditioned on a prompt and previous tokens in the output, and uses a decoding strategy such as greedy decoding, beam search, or nucleus sampling to select tokens at each position and assemble an output string. Like any abstractive generative model, LLMs risk outputting information that is false or unsupported with respect to a context or closed book knowledge, which is commonly called hallucination [1,2,3].

Recent work has observed that if multiple responses are sampled from a large language model, they are likely to hallucinate different values for each detail [3,4]. On the other hand, details that multiple sampled responses share in common are likely to be the truth.

In cases where a short answer can be easily parsed from a generated response, self consistency [4] uses voting (using exact matches of the parsed short answer) to select a better answer more reliably than an individual sample. However, this procedure does not apply to tasks where the full response is needed rather than just an extracted short answer.

Our main contribution is a novel decoding mechanism, applicable to any LLM task, which samples multiple text outputs from the LLM and selects the most consistent choice for each sentence, reflecting the commonality in the responses. We compare our decoding technique to several baselines in automatic factuality metrics, applied to Llama 2 (chat) and Mistral. We also contribute human evaluations, including a coarse classification of errors. In the accompanying code, we provide an implementation of our method and the baselines, together with the human evaluation dataset.
